groups.label: Siege of Quebec
groups.definition: Reports of the American siege of Quebec in the 1776 papers: Montgomery's letter calling on Carleton to surrender (December 1775), the account of the failed assault of 31 December, and a camp letter of 6 April 1776. Contains those three groups; the wider coverage is not included.

groups.label: Montgomery's letter to Carleton
groups.definition: Printings of General Montgomery's letter to Governor Carleton from before Quebec, dated December 1775, calling on him to surrender the town.

groups.label: Failed assault on Quebec
groups.definition: Printings of a Philadelphia report (25 January 1776) of the unsuccessful attempt to take Quebec by storm on 31 December 1775.

groups.label: Letter from the camp before Quebec
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from the American camp before Quebec, dated 6 April 1776, on the batteries and the want of men. It circulated in two versions.

groups.label: Boston evacuated
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from headquarters at Cambridge, 19 March 1776, reporting that the British army left Boston on 17 March.

groups.label: Hopkins's report from New Providence
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of Commodore Esek Hopkins's letter of 9 April 1776 to the President of Congress, on the fleet's expedition to New Providence in the Bahamas.

groups.label: Campbell's letter after his capture
groups.definition: Printings of Lieutenant Colonel Campbell's letter to General Howe (Boston, 19 June 1776), reporting that he and two companies of Highlanders had been taken in Boston harbour.

groups.label: Washington meets Colonel Patterson
groups.definition: Printings of the account of the interview of 20 July 1776 between General Washington and Colonel Patterson, General Howe's adjutant general.

groups.label: British warships in the Hudson
groups.definition: Reports of the British warships that went up the Hudson on 12 July 1776: lying in Haverstraw Bay, boats driven off at Tappan, the attack by American row galleys (3 August) and the fire-ship attack (16 August). Contains those four groups; the wider coverage is not included.

groups.label: Warships in Haverstraw Bay
groups.definition: Printings of a New York report (24 July 1776) that the men of war lie in Haverstraw Bay, that a tender was fired on, and that a landing party was attacked at Peekskill.

groups.label: Boats driven off at Tappan
groups.definition: Printings of a New York report (end of July 1776) that about fifteen inhabitants drove off five boats from the men of war trying to land on Tappan meadows.

groups.label: Row galleys attack the warships
groups.definition: Printings of an eyewitness account of the attack by American row galleys (gondolas) on the Phoenix and the Rose on 3 August 1776.

groups.label: Fire-ship attack
groups.definition: Printings of a New York report of the fire-ship attack on the British ships in the Hudson on 16 August 1776.

groups.label: Congress orders 88 battalions
groups.definition: Printings of Congress's resolutions of 16 September 1776 to raise eighty-eight battalions to serve during the war, with each state's quota and the bounties, plus one condensed report.

groups.label: Intelligence received in Congress, October 1776
groups.definition: Printings of the 'Intelligence received in Congress, October 21st, from the Middle and Northern Departments': General Mercer's raid on Staten Island and Arnold's fleet engaging the British on Lake Champlain on 11 October.

groups.label: The King's speech of October 1775
groups.definition: Printings of George III's speech opening the session of Parliament in October 1775, which the American papers printed from January 1776. The printings date the speech differently: the 26th in one, the 27th in another.

groups.label: A Dublin paper: British force coming
groups.definition: Printings of news brought to Philadelphia in May 1776 by a passenger from Europe with a Dublin paper of 2 March: that a large naval force was coming to America and was ordered to sail on 10 April, followed by London paragraphs from that paper. The forecast is a report, not an observed event.

groups.label: Ethan Allen at Cork
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Cork (January 1776) on the gifts collected for Colonel Ethan Allen and his fellow prisoners in the Solebay, with Allen's note of thanks.

groups.label: London's address to the King
groups.definition: Printings of the City of London's address and petition to the King against the war (St. James's, 22 March 1776), with the King's answer.

groups.label: The King's speech of May 1776
groups.definition: Printings of George III's speech closing the session of Parliament on 23 May 1776.

groups.label: Congress opens the ports
groups.definition: Printings of Congress's resolutions of 6 April 1776 opening American ports to trade with all countries not under the British crown.

groups.label: Rhode Island renounces allegiance
groups.definition: Printings of the Rhode Island General Assembly's act of May 1776 repealing the act that secured allegiance to the King and putting the colony's name in place of his in commissions and writs.

groups.label: Congress's resolution of 15 May
groups.definition: Printings of Congress's resolution of 15 May 1776, with its preamble, recommending that the colonies adopt governments under the authority of the people. Includes printings that quote it in full in reports of other bodies' proceedings.

groups.label: Virginia Convention, 15 May 1776
groups.definition: Printings of the Virginia Convention's resolutions of 15 May 1776, which instructed the colony's delegates to propose that Congress declare the colonies free and independent states.

groups.label: Pennsylvania's new instructions
groups.definition: Printings of the Pennsylvania Assembly's instructions of 8 June 1776 to its delegates in Congress, which withdrew the November instruction to reject any proposal that might lead to separation from Great Britain.

groups.label: Declaration of Independence
groups.definition: Printings of the Declaration of Independence (4 July 1776), plus one printing of its conclusion with a summary a week before that paper printed the full text.

groups.label: Congress on the Cedars cartel
groups.definition: Printings of the report adopted by Congress on 10 July 1776 on the cartel General Arnold agreed with Captain Foster after the surrender at the Cedars, with its resolutions.

groups.label: Prize resolutions extended
groups.definition: Printings of Congress's resolution of 24 July 1776 extending its earlier resolutions on captured ships and goods to all subjects of the King of Great Britain, except the inhabitants of the Bermudas and the Bahamas.

groups.label: Staten Island peace conference
groups.definition: Reports of the meeting of a committee of Congress (Franklin, John Adams and Edward Rutledge) with Lord Howe on Staten Island in September 1776: their setting off, and the committee's report to Congress. Contains those two groups.

groups.label: Committee sets off to meet Lord Howe
groups.definition: Printings of a Philadelphia report (September 1776) that Franklin, John Adams and Edward Rutledge had set off for New York to confer with Lord Howe.

groups.label: Committee's report on the conference
groups.definition: Printings of the committee's report to Congress on its meeting with Lord Howe on Staten Island, published by order of Congress in September 1776.

observations.excerpt: Captain Boye positively asserts, that previous to his failing, accounts were received at the custom-house of Liverpool, of 17 sail of French vessels, men of war and transports, having a number of troops on board, destined for a descent on Ireland, being through gusts of weather blown into Bantry Bay, most of them distressed; some of the people went on shore, were made prisoners, and sent to Dublin; from the situation of the place the whole must inevitably be captured. observations.excerpt: Capt. Boyd, positively asserts, that previous to his sailing, accounts were received at the custom house of Liverpool, of 17 sail of French vessels, men of war and transports, having a number of troops on board, destined for a DESCENT ON IRELAND, being through stress of weather, blown into Bantry Bay, most of them dismasted; some of the people went on shore, were made prisoners, and went to Dublin; from the situation of the place the whole must inevitably be captured. They intended to have effected a landing at Londonderry in the North of Ireland. [NOTE. Capt. Boyd failed from Liverpool on the 29th December, and the French fleet left Brest, on the 26th of the same month: How then is it possible they should have reached Ireland in 3 days, and the accounts from thence received at Liverpool? Can it be thought that 20,000 French troops, and 17 ships of the line, have surrendered to the inhabitants of Bantry, whose population does not exceed 10,000 souls? It is more natural to think the French have taken that town.—Why were those 20,000 French sent to Dublin, 154 miles from Bantry Bay, and not to Cork, that lies but 9 miles from it? Can it be presumed, that the French fleet, in order to effect a landing at Londonderry, had entered the channel of Ireland so full of dangers, instead of sailing westward, on the main; a route much shorter and less difficult, free from the dangers of the channel, and which would not have exposed them to discovery from Liverpool or Dublin, and meet with every obstacle, that could have frustrated their design. CHRONICLE.]

observations.note: Printed CHRONICLE challenge; objections are not independently adjudicated. Some failed forms read sailed in the scan.

observations.excerpt: Of the intelligence brought by the late arrivals, the most important relates to the French expedition against Ireland. By comparing the various accounts it appears, that the French failed from Brest with a view of invading Ireland. Their force consisted of about 50 sail, including transports, of which 17 were of the line and about 25,000 men on board. They failed in three divisions, under the command of De Galle, Bouvet and Neilly; the land troops under the orders of Gen. Hoche. They had scarcely left the port when bad weather dispersed them. Chief part of the fleet however, rendezvoused at Bantry Bay, but the frigate la Fraternite, on board of which were the commanders of the fleet and land forces not joining the fleet, after some delay they left the bay without molestation, except from the winds and by the best and latest accounts, reached Brest in divisions, without material loss. The Fraternite was one of the vessels to return. The expedition appears to have caused great alarm in Ireland and England. Had not the elements conspired against the French, little doubt can be entertained but they would have been successful. The expedition appears to have been planned on a large scale. The Toulon fleet which came round to L'Orient, and the armament at Dunkirk were probably to co-operate. The French appear still to have an expedition to Ireland in contemplation. A Paris date of January 29, mentions the arrival of Gen. Hoche in that capital, to give an account of his expedition.
observations.summary: Two weeks after printing Boyd's capture prediction, the Patowmac Guardian prints a summary saying the fleet dispersed and returned to Brest.
observations.note: The same summary the Kentucky Gazette printed on 19 April (H007), here 20 days earlier under a Martinsburg dateline. Neither paper names a source, so the copying route is unknown. The wording differs: Kentucky adds 'We have collected under this head…' and 'Notwithstanding the above failure'; this version adds the Fraternité's return, the 'great alarm' sentences and a Paris date about Hoche.

observations.excerpt: It is easy to perceive, that the American papers, cited in this decree, are the Jacobin Gazettes of the United States, and that the instances quoted, are seven out of eight, false and scandalous. It is also very evident, that the French Agents, in the United States, have published those very accounts in the Aurora , Argus , Chronicle , and other hiring papers, merely to give a pretext to the plunderers in the West-Indies, to seize and confiscate American vessels, and that the Printers of them have been base and sordid enough to send them those papers, in order that they may be adduced as documents, to justify their infamy! The American merchants and seamen, who suffer under the piracies in the West-Indies, now look to those Printers as the Authors of their misery; and were they to prosecute for reparation, an honest jury would do no less than grant a verdict in their favor.

observations.excerpt: BOSTON, OCT. 11. Fraternity.—Capt. Dunbar, from St. Croix, in lat. 23, N. long. 65, 35, W. was boarded by a French privateer brig, from Guadalupe, the capt. of which, with five of his crew, came on board and demanded Capt. D's papers; after examination, ordered his chests and trunks to be opened— took from them all the money and letters— took all the flock cabin stores, spare rigging, sails and blocks—one cask of rum, &c. —suffered his people to steal even knives and forks, spoons, tumblers, and every article remaining in the cabin. The privateer captain put on board us two seamen taken from the brig Favourite, Scituate, of Baltimore, and Mr. Taylor, supercargo, with a cargo of 50,000 dollars. He also wished to get rid of Capt. Scituate and Mr. Taylor, but they insisted on staying aboard the privateer and know the state of their property, which spirited behaviour produced a conduct unworthy a man, for on their refusal to quit the privateer, the capt. indignantly flogged them! Several other American masters and seamen were on board this privateer, among them was Mr. John Barnes, of Marblehead. Before the privateer left us, she took a loop from Rhode-Island, capt. Briggs, bound to Cape-Francois. The captain of the privateer to finish his brutal behaviour, threatened to punish capt. Dunbar—dismissed him with a curse on his country, and a determination to rob every American vessel that could not be made a prize of.

observations.note: A condensed paraphrase rather than the quoted statement, so it belongs to the boarding group but not the core report group.

observations.excerpt: Same day, brig Peace and Plenty, Dunbar, St. Croix, 24 days. In lat. 23, N. long. 65, 55, W. was boarded by a French privateer brig, from Guadalupe, under English colors. The particulars of the treatment which Capt. D. received, is thus recorded by him. "The capt. of this privateer came on board, with five of his crew, and demanded my papers; after examination, ordered all my trunks and chests to be opened, and took from them all the money they contained, with the letters, which he opened; he took all our stock, and cabin stores, with all the spare running rigging, sails and blocks, and cut one studling-fall from the yard; he also took one cask of rum, belonging to the cargo, and a case that belonged to capt. Haynes, who was to have come passenger, contents unknown. After plundering us of the above articles, he suffered his people to rob us of what they pleased, and so fully devoted were they to the business of thieving, that they took every article they could find, even to the knives, forks, spoons and tumblers, and in fact every article remaining in the cabin.—He then put two seamen on board, that were taken a few days before from the brig Favorite, Sisson, of Baltimore, master, and Mr. Taylor, supercargo, with a cargo of 50,000 dollars. The capt. of the privateer, wished to put capt. Sisson, and Mr. Taylor on board my vessel, but they insisted on staying aboard the privateer, and demanded to know the fate of their property, which spirited behaviour produced on the commander of the privateer, a conduct unworthy a man, for on their refusal to quit the privateer he inhumanly flogged them! Besides capt. Sisson, there were several other American masters and seamen on board the privateer, names, except one, not to be ascertained, this individual's name was John Barnes, of Marblehead:—A few hours previous to our being boarded, the privateer took a sloop from Rhode-Island, capt. Briggs, bound to Cape Francois, who, he said, was a good prize. To add insult to our misfortune this inhuman pirate threatened to take me on board his vessel, and inflict an ignominious punishment on me; and finished his brutal behaviour by dismissing me, with a curse on my country, and a declared determination to rob every American vessel he could not make a prize of.

observations.excerpt: Dreadful SHIPWRECK!! The following account of the shipwreck of the Two Sisters of Rhode-Island, is taken from a Hand-Bill published at BANTRY-BAY, AUG. 12, '97. This morning about 2 o'clock, as some of our fishing boats were working out between the heads, they saw a large ship in the Offing, seemingly in great distress. They stood for the ship, and about 10 o'clock, they boarded her; but there was only one living man on board. She proves to be the Two Sisters, from Rhode-Island, bound for Bristol, and had been out five weeks:—Such a wreck, surely never was seen before! her mizen-mast was all split to pieces, and her main-mast was a stern hanging by some of the wreck; her foremast was also split to pieces, and her fore-top-mast gone by the cap in her steerage or half deck. There were seven men burnt to a coal, and the mate lying under the windlass dead; and as for the Captain, we have no account of him, only the young man found with the wreck says that the Captain and all hands were on deck when some dreadful thunder and lightning came on; and that there were six men on the main-top-sail yard when the mainmast went over the side, and that they were all lost. He says the Captain was on the quarter deck when the mast went, but as he did not see him afterwards, he thinks the wreck hauled him overboard.
observations.summary: The New Hampshire Gazette reprints a Bantry Bay hand-bill dated 12 August 1797 on the wreck of the Rhode Island ship Two Sisters.
observations.note: Hand-bill account: lightning struck the ship, one man survived, seven men were burnt and the mate died. The captain is missing.

observations.excerpt: A melancholy narrative appears in the lists of the disasters of the American ship Two Sisters, of Rhode-Island, bound for Bristol, off Bantry Bay, in August last. On appearance of distress, she was boarded by some people from the land—they found her mizen mast shivered to pieces, her main mast overboard, hanging astern, and her fore topsail gone by the cap—only one living man was found in the wreck, who informed that the ship had been struck by lightning, and that there were six men on the main topsail yard when the mainmast went over the side, all of whom were lost, together with the master of the vessel, who was wanted overboard—seven men were burnt to a coal, and the mate dead; the ship had four feet water in her hold when boarded—was from the Bay of Honduras, with oil, whale bone, logwood and mahogany; the captain's name Gilbert; owner Mr. Mosely of Rhode Island—the people of the coast hauled the vessel up on the beach; the bottom appeared to be in tolerable condition; but masts, spars, sails, &c. worth nothing.

observations.note: Different wording from the hand-bill, but the details correspond: six men on the main topsail yard, seven men burnt and the mate dead.

observations.excerpt: January 27. MELANCHOLLY AND DISTRESSING. This morning about a quarter before 6 o'clock, Fire broke out in the lower part of the Dwelling-House of Mr. Andrew Brown, Printer, of this city. The usual spirited exertions of the Citizens prevented the flames from extending to the adjoining houses—and Mr. Brown's Printing Office escaped uninjured. Every humane bosom must be wrung with anguish at the recital of the shocking catastrophe consequent to this event. Mr. Brown, his apprentices, and some other domestics of the family escaped with their lives, by rushing thro' the flames or jumping from the windows—Mr. Brown is very much bruised and is dangerously ill

observations.excerpt: PHILADELPHIA, Jan. 28. Melancholy Event. Never since we have assumed the office of recording passing events to the public, have we entered on the task with more painful sensations, than on the melancholy occasion we have now to mention. About 5 o'clock yesterday morning the house of Mr. ANDREW BROWN, Printer of the Philadelphia Gazette, in this city, was discovered to be on fire. How it originated or progressed, we have not correct information, but the melancholy and almost unparalleled catastrophe, is, we fear, too certain. Mrs. BROWN, two daughters, one son, and a negro boy, have perished in the flames. Two apprentices have suffered severely, and Mr. BROWN is so dreadfully burnt, that but faint hopes of his recovery are entertained.
